## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## plugin:figma:figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f… [truncated]

- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.

Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://goreleaser.com/static/schema.json
version: 2

before:
  hooks:
    - go mod tidy

builds:
  - id: harnaas
    main: ./cmd/harnaas
    binary: harnaas
    env:
      - CGO_ENABLED=0
    goos:
      - darwin
      - linux
      - windows
    goarch:
      - amd64
      - arm64
    ldflags:
      - -s -w
      # These stamps are what make `harnaas --version` report a release
      # version; an unstamped build falls back to the embedded build info.
      - -X github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/versioninfo.Version={{.Version}}
      - -X github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/versioninfo.Commit={{.ShortCommit}}

archives:
  - formats:
      - tar.gz
    format_overrides:
      - goos: windows
        formats:
          - zip

checksum:
  name_template: checksums.txt

changelog:
  use: github
  sort: asc
  filters:
    exclude:
      - "^docs:"
      - "^test:"
      - "^chore:"

release:
  # A tag carrying a pre-release suffix — v1.0.0-rc.1 — is published as a
  # GitHub pre-release without anybody having to remember a flag, and does not
  # become the "latest" release a bare download URL resolves to. The two
  # package managers below key off the same distinction.
  prerelease: auto
  make_latest: true

# The two package managers harnaas is distributed through. Each publishes into
# its own repository under the same organization, which is why both need a
# token of their own: the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN is scoped to the repository
# the workflow runs in, and neither of these pushes lands there.
#
# The token is read from the environment rather than named as a secret here,
# because .goreleaser.yaml is also run locally — a developer checking the
# config with `goreleaser check` or building a snapshot must not need one.

# A cask rather than a formula. `brews` is formally deprecated as of GoReleaser
# v2.16 and fails `goreleaser check`: a formula that only unpacks a pre-compiled
# binary was a workaround for Homebrew having no other way to ship one, and it
# no longer is. A cask is what Homebrew wants for a released binary today.
homebrew_casks:
  - name: harnaas
    repository:
      owner: harnaas
      name: homebrew-tap
      branch: main
      token: "{{ .Env.GORELEASER_TOKEN }}"
    # Homebrew reads Casks/ in a tap. It is also the default, and stating it
    # keeps the layout readable from this file rather than from the docs.
    directory: Casks
    homepage: https://github.com/harnaas/harnaas
    description: Manage a project's AI-harness assets as a declared, versioned dependency
    # A pre-release must never become what `brew install harnaas` resolves to:
    # "auto" skips the cask update for exactly the tags `release.prerelease`
    # above marks, so the two cannot disagree.
    skip_upload: auto
    hooks:
      post:
        # macOS quarantines anything downloaded by a program, and the binary is
        # not signed by an identified developer, so without this the first run
        # is refused by Gatekeeper with a message about an unverified developer
        # rather than anything a user can act on. The guard is what lets the
        # same cask install on Linux, where the attribute does not exist.
        install: |
          if OS.mac?
            system_command "/usr/bin/xattr", args: ["-dr", "com.apple.quarantine", "#{staged_path}/harnaas"]
          end

scoops:
  - name: harnaas
    repository:
      owner: harnaas
      name: scoop-bucket
      branch: main
      token: "{{ .Env.GORELEASER_TOKEN }}"
    # Scoop reads a bucket/ directory when one exists and the repository root
    # otherwise; committing to the directory now avoids a move later.
    directory: bucket
    homepage: https://github.com/harnaas/harnaas
    description: Manage a project's AI-harness assets as a declared, versioned dependency
    skip_upload: auto

file.content:
name: Release

# Every action below is pinned to a commit SHA with the tag in a trailing
# comment, for the reason ci.yml gives: a tag is mutable, and a mutable
# third-party action runs with this repository's token. That matters more here
# than in CI — this workflow holds a token that can write to two other
# repositories.
on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v*'

# Read by default, with the one job that needs to write asking for it below.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      # Creating the GitHub release and uploading its archives. This grant does
      # not extend to homebrew-tap or scoop-bucket, which is why the release
      # also needs GORELEASER_TOKEN.
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          # The changelog is built from the commits between this tag and the
          # previous one, and the version is derived from the tag itself, so a
          # shallow clone produces an empty changelog and a wrong version.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-go@b7ad1dad31e06c5925ef5d2fc7ad053ef454303e # v7.0.0
        with:
          # Track go.mod so a Go bump does not need a parallel workflow edit.
          go-version-file: go.mod

      # goreleaser is pinned in mise.toml and run through mise rather than
      # through goreleaser-action, so the version that validates the config in
      # CI and the version that builds the release are the same one. An action
      # with its own version input would be a second place to keep in step, and
      # the two only ever disagree on release day.
      - uses: jdx/mise-action@f10502fc09dadecfefb962fff68ce77213930204 # v4

      - name: Build and publish the release
        run: mise run release
        env:
          # Creates the release on this repository and uploads its archives.
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          # Pushes the cask to harnaas/homebrew-tap and the manifest to
          # harnaas/scoop-bucket. A fine-grained token scoped to those two
          # repositories with Contents: read and write, and nothing else.
          GORELEASER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GORELEASER_TOKEN }}

#!/bin/sh
#MISE description="Build and publish the release for the current tag"

set -eu

# The Homebrew cask and the Scoop manifest are pushed into harnaas/homebrew-tap
# and harnaas/scoop-bucket, which the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN cannot reach:
# it is scoped to the repository the workflow runs in. Checking for the token
# here rather than letting the template fail turns goreleaser's "map has no
# entry for key GORELEASER_TOKEN" into a sentence naming the secret to set.
#
# The check is a refusal rather than a warning because a release that published
# the archives and silently skipped both package managers is the failure that
# is hardest to notice: `brew upgrade` simply keeps reporting the old version.
if [ -z "${GORELEASER_TOKEN:-}" ]; then
  echo "GORELEASER_TOKEN is not set, so the Homebrew cask and the Scoop manifest cannot be published." >&2
  echo >&2
  echo "Set it as a repository secret with:" >&2
  echo "  gh secret set GORELEASER_TOKEN --repo harnaas/harnaas" >&2
  exit 1
fi

goreleaser release --clean

=== homebrew-tap README ===
# harnaas Homebrew tap

The Homebrew tap for [harnaas](https://github.com/harnaas/harnaas) — a Go CLI that manages a
project's AI-harness assets as a declared, versioned dependency.

## Install

```sh
brew tap harnaas/tap
brew install --cask harnaas
```

Or in one command, without tapping first:

```sh
brew install --cask harnaas/tap/harnaas
```

Verify:

```sh
harnaas --version
```

## Upgrade

```sh
brew update
brew upgrade --cask harnaas
```

## Uninstall

```sh
brew uninstall --cask harnaas
brew untap harnaas/tap
```

## Supported platforms

The cask carries a build for each of these, selected automatically:

| OS | Architectures |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | Intel (`amd64`), Apple silicon (`arm64`) |
| Linux | `amd64`, `arm64` |

Homebrew on Linux installs this cask too — the generated cask carries `on_linux` blocks pointing at
the Linux archives, so `brew install --cask harnaas` works on both platforms.

## Why a cask and not a formula

A formula that only unpacks a pre-compiled binary was a workaround for Homebrew having no other way
to ship one, and it no longer is. GoReleaser formally deprecated its formula output in v2.16 in
favour of casks, which is what Homebrew wants for a released binary today.

One consequence is worth stating: because the binaries are not signed by an identified developer,
macOS would quarantine them and Gatekeeper would refuse the first run with a message about an
unverified developer. The cask carries a `postflight` hook that clears the quarantine attribute, so
that never surfaces.

## This repository is generated

**Do not edit `Casks/harnaas.rb` by hand.** It is written by
[GoReleaser](https://goreleaser.com) from
[`.goreleaser.yaml`](https://github.com/harnaas/harnaas/blob/main/.goreleaser.yaml) in the main
repository, on every tagged release, and any manual edit is overwritten by the next one. The file
says so in its first line.

A release carrying a pre-release suffix — `v1.0.0-rc.1` — deliberately does not update the cask, so
`brew install` never resolves to a release candidate.

Issues and pull requests belong on [harnaas/harnaas](https://github.com/harnaas/harnaas).

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the "casks are not supported" error on Linux with Homebrew:

## The Issue

Casks are only for macOS, and cask does not yet work on any Linux distributions. When you attempt to use `brew install --cask` on Linux, you'll encounter an error message stating that casks are not supported.

## Why This Happens

On macOS, the Homebrew cask subcommand offers users a way to install and manage entire applications using the same great command-line utility, but this functionality is not available for Linux systems. The error occurs because Homebrew's cask system is designed exclusively for macOS environments.

## Recent Developments

It's worth noting that there have been recent discussions about potentially adding Linux support for casks. Linux binaries are now allowed in casks, and are even being added to them in the official tap, suggesting that the Homebrew team has been exploring ways to extend cask support to Linux. However, as of now, this remains a macOS-only feature.

If you're on Linux and need to install software, you'll need to use alternative methods such as traditional Homebrew formulas or other package managers available for your Linux distribution.

# Linux Cask Support Status

Based on the GitHub issue content, **Linux cask support has not yet been fully implemented** in `brew bundle`, though the underlying infrastructure has been added to Homebrew itself.

## Current Status

The issue was opened on **February 25, 2025** and remains marked as "in progress" with assignee MikeMcQuaid. The problem is that while casks can be installed directly on Linux via `brew install --cask`, attempting to install them through `brew bundle` results in a skip warning: "Skipping cask font-fira-code-nerd-font (on Linux)".

## Key Finding

The reporter notes that "Linux binaries are now allowed in casks" following a recent pull request (#19121), and font casks are actively being added to the official tap. However, `brew bundle` still contains explicit checks that prevent cask installation on Linux, specifically in the skipper.rb file that would need modification to enable this functionality.

The issue indicates the technical capability exists; the blocker is removing or updating the Linux-specific restrictions within the bundle tool itself.

content.content:
# PR #19121: Linux Binary Support in Homebrew Casks

## Summary

This pull request was **merged on February 17, 2025** into Homebrew's main branch. It fundamentally changed how casks work on Linux systems.

## What Changed

The PR introduced support for Linux binaries in Homebrew casks, enabling functionality that was previously macOS-only. Key modifications include:

- **Binary installation on Linux**: Casks containing only binary or zap blocks became installable on Linux systems
- **Platform-specific blocks**: Added `on_linux` blocks alongside existing macOS functionality
- **SHA256 handling**: Implemented Linux-specific checksum support with bottle naming conventions
- **Zap support**: Extended the zap (uninstall cleanup) functionality to work on Linux

## Impact

As one developer noted, "casks that only have binary or zap will be installable on Linux" after this merge. However, there's an important caveat: installations are possible only when explicitly using `--cask` flag without relying on the API, preventing unwanted macOS-only binaries from being installed on Linux systems.

The merge also triggered a companion PR that added implicit macOS dependencies to existing casks without explicit `depends_on` declarations, protecting legacy packages from incompatibility issues.

## Future Direction

The implementation intentionally deferred API support and removal of macOS-version-specific logic for later work, focusing first on core functionality and real-world cask compatibility.

All three commands work end to end. Everything documented below is implemented and tested; where a
capability is deliberately absent — a renderer the contract names but nobody has written, a harness
with no adapter — it is described as what it is rather than as a gap.

One thing harnaas does not do, by choice rather than omission: no forge other than GitHub. Named
adapters exist for `claude-code` and `devin-cli`, and most harnesses need no adapter at all — see
[Where assets land](#where-assets-land). Both registries exist so that adding either a forge or an
adapter is additive rather than a reshaping.

## Installation

### macOS and Linux, with Homebrew

```sh
brew tap harnaas/tap
brew install --cask harnaas
```

A cask rather than a formula, and it installs on Linux too — the generated cask carries `on_linux`
blocks pointing at the Linux archives. See the
[tap](https://github.com/harnaas/homebrew-tap) for why.

### Windows, with Scoop

```powershell
scoop bucket add harnaas https://github.com/harnaas/scoop-bucket
scoop install harnaas
```

### With Go

```sh
go install github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas@latest
```

This puts `harnaas` in `$(go env GOPATH)/bin`. Make sure that directory is on your `PATH`.

Requires Go 1.26.5 or newer — keep it aligned with the `go` directive in [`go.mod`](go.mod).

> **Until the first release above `v0.8.42`, this route does not work.** This repository was seeded
> from the entire.io CLI carrying that project's tags, and they were pushed before the history was
> rewritten. The tags are gone from the remote but the Go module proxy is immutable, so `@latest`
> still resolves to `v0.8.42` — a version whose `go.mod` reads `module github.com/entireio/cli` and
> which contains no `cmd/harnaas`. Only a tag above it takes the module path back. Homebrew and
> Scoop are unaffected: they resolve release assets, not the module proxy.

### From source

The repository uses [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/) as its single toolchain and task runner, which
pins the Go, golangci-lint, shellcheck and goreleaser versions for you:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/harnaas/harnaas.git
cd harnaas
mise install        # installs the pinned toolchain
mise run build      # produces ./harnaas (./harnaas.exe on Windows)
```

Or without mise:

```sh
go build -o harnaas ./cmd/harnaas
```

### Release binaries

Releases are built by [goreleaser](.goreleaser.yaml) for darwin, linux and windows on both amd64 and
arm64. Only a release build carries a stamped version; every other build self-reports what it can
recover from Go's embedded build information, so `harnaas --version` is always truthful about which
binary you are running.

### Verifying the install

```console
$ harnaas --version
harnaas 0.0.0-20260811105907-14edd937dd6a+dirty (14edd937dd6ac4ace33b6fa39b3f0a0f8ff88d34)
```

A release build reports its tag instead, e.g. `harnaas 1.2.0 (a1b2c3d)`.

# Releasing

Pushing a tag matching `v*` is the whole release. [`release.yml`](../.github/workflows/release.yml)
runs `mise run release`, which runs `goreleaser release --clean`, which builds the archives, creates
the GitHub release here, and writes a Homebrew cask and a Scoop manifest into two other
repositories. Nothing else is manual, and nothing in either of those repositories is edited by hand.

## What a release writes, and where

| Destination | Artifact | Written with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `harnaas/harnaas` | the release, six archives, `checksums.txt` | `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| `harnaas/homebrew-tap` | `Casks/harnaas.rb` | `GORELEASER_TOKEN` |
| `harnaas/scoop-bucket` | `bucket/harnaas.json` | `GORELEASER_TOKEN` |

Two credentials, because they reach two different places. Actions supplies `GITHUB_TOKEN` on its own
and it is scoped to the repository the workflow runs in — which is exactly why it cannot publish the
cask or the manifest, and why the second token exists.

The archives cover darwin, linux and windows on both amd64 and arm64. The version and commit are
stamped into the binary through `-X` ldflags, so a release build reports its tag from
`harnaas --version` rather than falling back to Go's embedded build information.

## One-time setup: `GORELEASER_TOKEN`

Until this secret is set, a tag push fails at [`mise-tasks/release`](../mise-tasks/release), before
goreleaser starts. That refusal is deliberate: a release that published the archives and silently
skipped both package managers is the failure hardest to notice, because `brew upgrade` just keeps
reporting the old version.

1. Open <https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new>.
2. **Resource owner: `harnaas`** — the organization, not your user account. The two repositories are
   org-owned, and a token owned by your account cannot be granted access to them. This is the step
   that is easy to get wrong, because the form defaults to your own account.
3. **Repository access → Only select repositories →** `harnaas/homebrew-tap` and
   `harnaas/scoop-bucket`. Deliberately *not* `harnaas/harnaas`: the release there is created by the
   workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so granting this token access to it would widen the blast radius
   for nothing.
4. **Repository permissions → Contents: Read and write.** Nothing else. `Metadata: Read-only` is
   added for you and is the only other permission the push needs.
5. Pick an expiration you will survive — see [When it stops working](#when-it-stops-working).
6. If the organization requires approval for fine-grained tokens, an owner must approve it under
   **Organization settings → Personal access tokens → Pending requests**. Until then the token
   exists and is denied, which is not distinguishable from a token that was never created.
7. Set it as a repository secret:

   ```sh
   gh secret set GORELEASER_TOKEN --repo harnaas/harnaas
   ```

   Paste at the prompt rather than passing `--body`, which would leave the token in your shell
   history.

8. Confirm it landed:

   ```sh
   gh secret list --repo harnaas/harnaas
   ```

## Cutting a release

```sh
git tag -a v0.9.0 -m 'v0.9.0'
git push origin v0.9.0
```

Two constraints on the number.

**The first tag must be above `v0.8.42`.** This repository was seeded from the entire.io CLI
carrying that project's tags. They are gone from the remote, but the Go module proxy is immutable,
so `go install …@latest` still resolves to `v0.8.42` — a version whose `go.mod` names a different
module and which contains no `cmd/harnaas`. Only a tag above it takes the module path back. Homebrew
and Scoop are unaffected either way: they resolve release assets, not the module proxy.

**A pre-release suffix changes who sees it.** `v1.0.0-rc.1` is published as a GitHub pre-release, is
not what a bare download URL resolves to, and updates *neither* the cask nor the Scoop manifest —
`release.prerelease: auto` and `skip_upload: auto` key off the same distinction, so the three cannot
disagree. A release candidate is therefore installable by URL and never by `brew install`.

The workflow does not run the test suite; it builds the tag it was given. Tag a commit that has
already gone green on `main`.

## Verifying

```sh
gh run watch --repo harnaas/harnaas
gh release view v0.9.0 --repo harnaas/harnaas
```

Then confirm both package managers actually received a commit — the release succeeding does not by
itself mean they did:

```sh
gh api repos/harnaas/homebrew-tap/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
gh api repos/harnaas/scoop-bucket/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
```

And end to end, on a machine that has them:

```sh
brew update && brew install --cask harnaas && harnaas --version
scoop update && scoop install harnaas; harnaas --version
```

## When it stops working

The token is the part that fails on a day nobody touched the repository.

An expired token, a revoked one, and one whose org approval was withdrawn all present identically:
GitHub answers the push with `404` rather than `403`, because it will not confirm to an
unauthorized caller that a repository exists. So the diagnostic to expect is not "permission
denied" but "not found" against a repository that plainly does exist.

The shape of that failure is worth knowing in advance. The GitHub release is created *before* the
two package managers are updated, so a token that has gone bad leaves a published release, two stale
taps, and a red workflow run. Nothing rolls back. The fix is to repair the token and re-run the
failed job — goreleaser re-publishes the cask and the manifest for the same tag without needing a
new one.

The other failure is quieter and is the one the guard in `mise-tasks/release` exists to prevent: the
secret missing entirely. That refuses before anything is built, and names the command to fix it.

## Checking the config without releasing

`goreleaser check` runs on every CI build through `mise run lint:goreleaser`, and fails on a
deprecated property as well as an invalid one — a release config is otherwise exercised once, on the
day a tag is pushed, which is the worst moment to learn that a property was renamed two minor
versions ago.

To exercise the whole build locally, including the generated cask and manifest, without publishing
anything or needing a token:

```sh
mise exec -- goreleaser release --snapshot --clean
```

The cask lands at `dist/homebrew/Casks/harnaas.rb` and the manifest at `dist/scoop/bucket/harnaas.json`.
Both are what a real release would push, with a snapshot version in place of the tag.

# Default `mode` Value and Re-run Behavior

According to the documentation, the default value for `mode` is **`keep-existing`**.

The configuration states:

> "Default: `keep-existing`."

## What Happens on Re-run

When you re-execute `goreleaser release` for a tag whose GitHub release already exists, the behavior depends on the `mode` setting:

- **`keep-existing`** (default): The existing release notes remain unchanged. GoReleaser will not modify them.
- **`append`**: New release notes get added after the existing content.
- **`prepend`**: New release notes are inserted before existing content.
- **`replace`**: Existing notes are completely overwritten with newly generated ones.

The documentation also notes an important caveat: "If you create the release before running GoReleaser, and the said release has some text in its body, GoReleaser will not override it with its release notes, unless you configure it to do so."

I found several relevant results about the "Resource not accessible by personal access token" 403 error with fine-grained tokens:

## Common Causes

The PAT may lack the exact permission (e.g., Pull requests: write) the operation requires. The fine-grained PAT does not include the target repository in its allowed list.

A call fails with 403 when the token has access to the repo but not the specific permission (contents, pull-requests, issues, etc.) the call needs.

## Solutions

For writing to public repositories, ensure the fine-grained PAT has access to that repo and "Contents: Read and Write". Edit the fine-grained PAT under Developer settings and add the specific repository with the exact permission (e.g., Contents: write, Pull requests: write).

Additionally, to open a PR, you need a token with the resource owner being the target, but unless you own the target repo or are a member of its owning organisation, it's not possible to create such a PAT.

Some users have resolved this by using classic tokens instead of fine-grained tokens.

   added for you and is the only other permission the push needs.
5. Pick an expiration you will survive — see [When it stops working](#when-it-stops-working).
6. If the organization requires approval for fine-grained tokens, an owner must approve it under
   **Organization settings → Personal access tokens → Pending requests**. Until then the token
   exists and is denied, which is not distinguishable from a token that was never created.
7. Set it as a repository secret:

   ```sh
   gh secret set GORELEASER_TOKEN --repo harnaas/harnaas
   ```

   Paste at the prompt rather than passing `--body`, which would leave the token in your shell
   history.

8. Confirm it landed:

   ```sh
   gh secret list --repo harnaas/harnaas
   ```

## Cutting a release

```sh
git tag -a v0.9.0 -m 'v0.9.0'
git push origin v0.9.0
```

Two constraints on the number.

**The first tag must be above `v0.8.42`.** This repository was seeded from the entire.io CLI
carrying that project's tags. They are gone from the remote, but the Go module proxy is immutable,
so `go install …@latest` still resolves to `v0.8.42` — a version whose `go.mod` names a different
module and which contains no `cmd/harnaas`. Only a tag above it takes the module path back. Homebrew
and Scoop are unaffected either way: they resolve release assets, not the module proxy.

**A pre-release suffix changes who sees it.** `v1.0.0-rc.1` is published as a GitHub pre-release, is
not what a bare download URL resolves to, and updates *neither* the cask nor the Scoop manifest —
`release.prerelease: auto` and `skip_upload: auto` key off the same distinction, so the three cannot
disagree. A release candidate is therefore installable by URL and never by `brew install`.

The workflow does not run the test suite; it builds the tag it was given. Tag a commit that has
already gone green on `main`.

## Verifying

```sh
gh run watch --repo harnaas/harnaas
gh release view v0.9.0 --repo harnaas/harnaas
```

Then confirm both package managers actually received a commit — the release succeeding does not by
itself mean they did:

```sh
gh api repos/harnaas/homebrew-tap/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
gh api repos/harnaas/scoop-bucket/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
```

And end to end, on a machine that has them:

```sh
brew update && brew install --cask harnaas && harnaas --version
scoop update && scoop install harnaas; harnaas --version
```

## When it stops working

The token is the part that fails on a day nobody touched the repository.

An expired token, a revoked one, and one whose org approval was withdrawn all present identically:
GitHub answers the push with `404` rather than `403`, because it will not confirm to an
unauthorized caller that a repository exists. So the diagnostic to expect is not "permission
denied" but "not found" against a repository that plainly does exist.

The shape of that failure is worth knowing in advance. The GitHub release is created *before* the
two package managers are updated, so a token that has gone bad leaves a published release, two stale
taps, and a red workflow run. Nothing rolls back. The fix is to repair the token and re-run the
failed job — goreleaser re-publishes the cask and the manifest for the same tag without needing a
new one.

The other failure is quieter and is the one the guard in `mise-tasks/release` exists to prevent: the
secret missing entirely. That refuses before anything is built, and names the command to fix it.

## Checking the config without releasing

`goreleaser check` runs on every CI build through `mise run lint:goreleaser`, and fails on a
deprecated property as well as an invalid one — a release config is otherwise exercised once, on the
day a tag is pushed, which is the worst moment to learn that a property was renamed two minor
versions ago.

To exercise the whole build locally, including the generated cask and manifest, without publishing
anything or needing a token:

```sh
mise exec -- goreleaser release --snapshot --clean
```

The cask lands at `dist/homebrew/Casks/harnaas.rb` and the manifest at `dist/scoop/bucket/harnaas.json`.
Both are what a real release would push, with a snapshot version in place of the tag.

# Git Sub-block Configuration for SSH Push

According to the documentation, the `git` sub-block under `repository` supports three fields:

1. **`url`**: "The Git URL to push" (supports templates)
2. **`private_key`**: "This can either be a path or the key contents" (supports templates)
3. **`ssh_command`**: "The value to be passed to `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`" with a default of `'ssh -i {{ .KeyPath }} -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -F /dev/null'` (supports templates)

## Important Constraint

The documentation emphasizes: "IMPORTANT: the key must not be password-protected" and warns "do not expose your private key in the configuration file!"

## YAML Example for SSH Push

```yaml
repository:
  git:
    url: 'ssh://[email protected]:repo.git'
    private_key: '{{ .Env.PRIVATE_KEY_PATH }}'
    ssh_command: 'ssh -i {{ .Env.KEY }} -o SomeOption=yes'
```

The `private_key` field accepts either a file path or the actual key contents, both passed through the template engine. The example shown uses an environment variable reference to keep secrets secure rather than hardcoding them.

# Releasing

Pushing a tag matching `v*` is the whole release. [`release.yml`](../.github/workflows/release.yml)
runs `mise run release`, which runs `goreleaser release --clean`, which builds the archives, creates
the GitHub release here, and writes a Homebrew cask and a Scoop manifest into two other
repositories. Nothing else is manual, and nothing in either of those repositories is edited by hand.

## What a release writes, and where

| Destination | Artifact | Written with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `harnaas/harnaas` | the release, six archives, `checksums.txt` | `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| `harnaas/homebrew-tap` | `Casks/harnaas.rb` | `GORELEASER_TOKEN` |
| `harnaas/scoop-bucket` | `bucket/harnaas.json` | `GORELEASER_TOKEN` |

Two credentials, because they reach two different places. Actions supplies `GITHUB_TOKEN` on its own
and it is scoped to the repository the workflow runs in — which is exactly why it cannot publish the
cask or the manifest, and why the second token exists.

The archives cover darwin, linux and windows on both amd64 and arm64. The version and commit are
stamped into the binary through `-X` ldflags, so a release build reports its tag from
`harnaas --version` rather than falling back to Go's embedded build information.

## One-time setup: `GORELEASER_TOKEN`

Until this secret is set, a tag push fails at [`mise-tasks/release`](../mise-tasks/release), before
goreleaser starts. That refusal is deliberate: a release that published the archives and silently
skipped both package managers is the failure hardest to notice, because `brew upgrade` just keeps
reporting the old version.

1. Open <https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new>.
2. **Resource owner: `harnaas`** — the organization, not your user account. The two repositories are
   org-owned, and a token owned by your account cannot be granted access to them. This is the step
   that is easy to get wrong, because the form defaults to your own account.
3. **Repository access → Only select repositories →** `harnaas/homebrew-tap` and
   `harnaas/scoop-bucket`. Deliberately *not* `harnaas/harnaas`: the release there is created by the
   workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so granting this token access to it would widen the blast radius
   for nothing.
4. **Repository permissions → Contents: Read and write.** Nothing else. `Metadata: Read-only` is
   added for you and is the only other permission the push needs.
5. Pick an expiration you will survive — see [When it stops working](#when-it-stops-working).
6. If the organization requires approval for fine-grained tokens, an owner must approve it under
   **Organization settings → Personal access tokens → Pending requests**. Until then the token
   exists and is denied, which is not distinguishable from a token that was never created.
7. Set it as a repository secret:

   ```sh
   gh secret set GORELEASER_TOKEN --repo harnaas/harnaas
   ```

   Paste at the prompt rather than passing `--body`, which would leave the token in your shell
   history.

8. Confirm it landed:

   ```sh
   gh secret list --repo harnaas/harnaas
   ```

## Cutting a release

```sh
git tag -a v0.9.0 -m 'v0.9.0'
git push origin v0.9.0
```

Two constraints on the number.

**The first tag must be above `v0.8.42`.** This repository was seeded from the entire.io CLI
carrying that project's tags. They are gone from the remote, but the Go module proxy is immutable,
so `go install …@latest` still resolves to `v0.8.42` — a version whose `go.mod` names a different
module and which contains no `cmd/harnaas`. Only a tag above it takes the module path back. Homebrew
and Scoop are unaffected either way: they resolve release assets, not the module proxy.

**A pre-release suffix changes who sees it.** `v1.0.0-rc.1` is published as a GitHub pre-release, is
not what a bare download URL resolves to, and updates *neither* the cask nor the Scoop manifest —
`release.prerelease: auto` and `skip_upload: auto` key off the same distinction, so the three cannot
disagree. A release candidate is therefore installable by URL and never by `brew install`.

The workflow does not run the test suite; it builds the tag it was given. Tag a commit that has
already gone green on `main`.

## Verifying

```sh
gh run watch --repo harnaas/harnaas
gh release view v0.9.0 --repo harnaas/harnaas
```

Then confirm both package managers actually received a commit — the release succeeding does not by
itself mean they did:

```sh
gh api repos/harnaas/homebrew-tap/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
gh api repos/harnaas/scoop-bucket/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
```

And end to end, on a machine that has them:

```sh
brew update && brew install --cask harnaas && harnaas --version
scoop update && scoop install harnaas; harnaas --version
```

## When it stops working

The token is the part that fails on a day nobody touched the repository, and it fails in two shapes
worth telling apart, because they need different fixes:

- **`401 Bad credentials`** — the token expired or was revoked. Mint a new one and re-set the
  secret.
- **`403 Resource not accessible by personal access token`** — the token is valid but is not
  granted what the push needs: the repository is missing from its list, `Contents` is not set to
  read *and* write, or the organization has not approved it. Both tap repositories are public, so
  there is no `404`-to-hide-existence case here; a `403` always means the grant, never the URL.

The shape of the failure is worth knowing in advance. The GitHub release is created *before* the two
package managers are updated — goreleaser publishes them last precisely because the cask and the
manifest need the release's download URLs — so a token that has gone bad leaves a published release,
two stale taps, and a red workflow run. Nothing rolls back.

The fix is to repair the token and re-run the failed job for the same tag. `release.mode` defaults to
`keep-existing`, so re-running leaves the existing release and its notes alone and re-publishes the
cask and the manifest. No new tag is needed.

The other failure is quieter and is the one the guard in `mise-tasks/release` exists to prevent: the
secret missing entirely. That refuses before anything is built, and names the command to fix it.

## Checking the config without releasing

`goreleaser check` runs on every CI build through `mise run lint:goreleaser`, and fails on a
deprecated property as well as an invalid one — a release config is otherwise exercised once, on the
day a tag is pushed, which is the worst moment to learn that a property was renamed two minor
versions ago.

To exercise the whole build locally, including the generated cask and manifest, without publishing
anything or needing a token:

```sh
mise exec -- goreleaser release --snapshot --clean
```

The cask lands at `dist/homebrew/Casks/harnaas.rb` and the manifest at `dist/scoop/bucket/harnaas.json`.
Both are what a real release would push, with a snapshot version in place of the tag.

My previous message claimed deploy keys were enabled. That was wrong, and the cause was my own bug: `gh api --jq` writes the error body to *stdout* on failure, and my probe treated any stdout as success, so the `422` read as an id. | Build, archives, cask, manifest, version stamp | verified working |

## The one thing I cannot do

<https://github.com/organizations/harnaas/settings/member_privileges> → **Deploy keys** → **Enabled**

New orgs default this off ([GA Oct 2024](https://github.blog/changelog/2024-10-23-repository-deploy-keys-are-controlled-by-enterprise-and-organization-policy-ga/)); yours was created 2026-07-31. Changing it needs `admin:org`, and your gh token has `gist, read:org, repo, workflow`. I have no route to it — this is a permission I hold none of, not a step I've skipped.

The moment you flip it, the watcher fires and I complete the rest with no further input: mint both ed25519 keys, install them write-scoped on each tap, set `HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY` and `SCOOP_BUCKET_DEPLOY_KEY` via stdin so neither key enters this transcript, swap in the validated config, update the guard in `mise-tasks/release` and `release.yml`, re-run `goreleaser check`, and verify each key authenticates against its own repo.

If you'd rather not wait on the toggle, the fine-grained PAT from earlier still works with the config exactly as it is on disk today — that path needs no repo changes at all.

input.content:
#!/bin/sh
#MISE description="Build and publish the release for the current tag"

set -eu

# The Homebrew cask and the Scoop manifest are pushed into harnaas/homebrew-tap
# and harnaas/scoop-bucket, which the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN cannot reach:
# it is scoped to the repository the workflow runs in. Each tap is pushed over
# SSH with a deploy key of its own, so there are two credentials here rather
# than one, and a run holding only one of them would publish one package
# manager and leave the other on the previous version.
#
# Checking here rather than letting the template fail turns goreleaser's "map
# has no entry for key HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY" into a sentence naming the
# secret to set. Both are reported in a single run for the reason harnaas
# accumulates validation violations rather than stopping at the first: two
# missing secrets are one trip to the settings page, not two.
#
# The check is a refusal rather than a warning because a release that published
# the archives and silently skipped a package manager is the failure hardest to
# notice — `brew upgrade` simply keeps reporting the old version.
missing=''
if [ -z "${HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY:-}" ]; then
  missing="${missing} HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY"
fi
if [ -z "${SCOOP_BUCKET_DEPLOY_KEY:-}" ]; then
  missing="${missing} SCOOP_BUCKET_DEPLOY_KEY"
fi

if [ -n "$missing" ]; then
  echo "The Homebrew cask and the Scoop manifest cannot be published." >&2
  echo >&2
  echo "Not set:" >&2
  for name in $missing; do
    echo "  ${name}" >&2
  done
  echo >&2
  echo "Each is the private half of a deploy key on the repository it pushes to." >&2
  echo "Recreate one with:" >&2
  echo "  ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ./k -C goreleaser" >&2
  echo "  gh api -X POST repos/harnaas/<tap-repo>/keys -f title=goreleaser \\" >&2
  echo "    -f key=\"\$(cat ./k.pub)\" -F read_only=false" >&2
  echo "  gh secret set <NAME> --repo harnaas/harnaas < ./k" >&2
  echo >&2
  echo "See docs/RELEASING.md." >&2
  exit 1
fi

goreleaser release --clean

name: Release

# comment, for the reason ci.yml gives: a tag is mutable, and a mutable
# third-party action runs with this repository's token. That matters more here
# than in CI — this workflow holds a token that can write to two other
# repositories.
on:

    tags:
      - 'v*'

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      # Creating the GitHub release and uploading its archives. This grant does
      # not extend to homebrew-tap or scoop-bucket, which is why the release
      # also needs GORELEASER_TOKEN.
      contents: write

          # previous one, and the version is derived from the tag itself, so a
          # shallow clone produces an empty changelog and a wrong version.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-go@b7ad1dad31e06c5925ef5d2fc7ad053ef454303e # v7.0.0

      # with its own version input would be a second place to keep in step, and
      # the two only ever disagree on release day.

input.content:
# Releasing

Pushing a tag matching `v*` is the whole release. [`release.yml`](../.github/workflows/release.yml)
runs `mise run release`, which runs `goreleaser release --clean`, which builds the archives, creates
the GitHub release here, and pushes a Homebrew cask and a Scoop manifest into two other
repositories. Nothing else is manual, and nothing in either of those repositories is edited by hand.

## What a release writes, and where

| Destination | Artifact | Written with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `harnaas/harnaas` | the release, six archives, `checksums.txt` | `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| `harnaas/homebrew-tap` | `Casks/harnaas.rb` | `HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY` |
| `harnaas/scoop-bucket` | `bucket/harnaas.json` | `SCOOP_BUCKET_DEPLOY_KEY` |

Three credentials, because they reach three different places. Actions supplies `GITHUB_TOKEN` on its
own and it is scoped to the repository the workflow runs in — which is exactly why it cannot publish
the cask or the manifest, and why the other two exist.

The archives cover darwin, linux and windows on both amd64 and arm64. The version and commit are
stamped into the binary through `-X` ldflags, so a release build reports its tag from
`harnaas --version` rather than falling back to Go's embedded build information.

## The credentials

Each tap is pushed over SSH with a **write-scoped deploy key of its own**, rather than with one
token granting `Contents: write` on both. That is two properties rather than one:

- A deploy key reaches exactly one repository. The credential that writes the cask cannot write the
  bucket, and neither grants anything else in the organization. A shared token has no such seam.
- A deploy key does not expire. A token does, and the release that first met an expired one would be
  the release that published the archives and silently left both package managers on the previous
  version — the failure that is hardest to notice, because `brew upgrade` simply keeps reporting the
  old version.

Both are already installed. `mise run release` refuses before goreleaser starts if either is
missing, naming the ones that are, so this never degrades into a half-published release.

### The organization policy this depends on

Deploy keys are an organization-level policy, and **new organizations default to disabled** — this
one did, and it was turned on to make the above possible. It lives at
<https://github.com/organizations/harnaas/settings/member_privileges> under **Deploy keys**.

Turning it back off does not merely prevent new keys: it **disables the existing ones**, in every
repository in the organization. Both taps stop accepting pushes and every release afterwards fails
at the publish step. If that policy has to change, migrate to a fine-grained token first — see
[Falling back to a token](#falling-back-to-a-token).

### Rotating or recreating a key

Per tap, substituting the repository and the secret name:

```sh
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ./k -C goreleaser
gh api -X POST repos/harnaas/homebrew-tap/keys \
  -f title="goreleaser (harnaas/harnaas release workflow)" \
  -f key="$(cat ./k.pub)" -F read_only=false
gh secret set HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY --repo harnaas/harnaas < ./k
rm -f ./k ./k.pub
```

`read_only=false` is the part that matters — a read-only key authenticates fine and then fails the
push. Pipe the private key into `gh secret set` from the file rather than pasting it, so it never
reaches your shell history. Delete the local copies afterwards; the secret is the only copy needed.

To confirm a key is bound to the repository you think it is:

```sh
ssh -i ./k -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -T git@github.com
# Hi harnaas/homebrew-tap! You've successfully authenticated, ...
```

## Cutting a release

```sh
git tag -a v0.9.0 -m 'v0.9.0'
git push origin v0.9.0
```

Two constraints on the number.

**The first tag must be above `v0.8.42`.** This repository was seeded from the entire.io CLI
carrying that project's tags. They are gone from the remote, but the Go module proxy is immutable,
so `go install …@latest` still resolves to `v0.8.42` — a version whose `go.mod` names a different
module and which contains no `cmd/harnaas`. Only a tag above it takes the module path back. Homebrew

runs `mise run release`, which runs `goreleaser release --clean`, which builds the archives, creates
the GitHub release here, and pushes a Homebrew cask and a Scoop manifest into two other
repositories. Nothing else is manual, and nothing in either of those repositories is edited by hand.

## What a release writes, and where

| Destination | Artifact | Written with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `harnaas/harnaas` | the release, six archives, `checksums.txt` | `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| `harnaas/homebrew-tap` | `Casks/harnaas.rb` | `HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY` |
| `harnaas/scoop-bucket` | `bucket/harnaas.json` | `SCOOP_BUCKET_DEPLOY_KEY` |

own and it is scoped to the repository the workflow runs in — which is exactly why it cannot publish
the cask or the manifest, and why the other two exist.

stamped into the binary through `-X` ldflags, so a release build reports its tag from
`harnaas --version` rather than falling back to Go's embedded build information.

```sh
git tag -a v0.9.0 -m 'v0.9.0'
git push origin v0.9.0
```

Two constraints on the number.

**The first tag must be above `v0.8.42`.** This repository was seeded from the entire.io CLI
carrying that project's tags. They are gone from the remote, but the Go module proxy is immutable,
so `go install …@latest` still resolves to `v0.8.42` — a version whose `go.mod` names a different
module and which contains no `cmd/harnaas`. Only a tag above it takes the module path back. Homebrew
and Scoop are unaffected either way: they resolve release assets, not the module proxy.

**A pre-release suffix changes who sees it.** `v1.0.0-rc.1` is published as a GitHub pre-release, is
not what a bare download URL resolves to, and updates *neither* the cask nor the Scoop manifest —
`release.prerelease: auto` and `skip_upload: auto` key off the same distinction, so the three cannot
disagree. A release candidate is therefore installable by URL and never by `brew install`.

The workflow does not run the test suite; it builds the tag it was given. Tag a commit that has
already gone green on `main`.

## Verifying

```sh
gh run watch --repo harnaas/harnaas
gh release view v0.9.0 --repo harnaas/harnaas
```

Then confirm both package managers actually received a commit — the release succeeding does not by
itself mean they did:

```sh
gh api repos/harnaas/homebrew-tap/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
gh api repos/harnaas/scoop-bucket/commits --jq '.[0].commit.message'
```

And end to end, on a machine that has them:

```sh
brew update && brew install --cask harnaas && harnaas --version
scoop update && scoop install harnaas; harnaas --version
```

## When it stops working

The token is the part that fails on a day nobody touched the repository, and it fails in two shapes
worth telling apart, because they need different fixes:

- **`401 Bad credentials`** — the token expired or was revoked. Mint a new one and re-set the
  secret.
- **`403 Resource not accessible by personal access token`** — the token is valid but is not
  granted what the push needs: the repository is missing from its list, `Contents` is not set to
  read *and* write, or the organization has not approved it. Both tap repositories are public, so
  there is no `404`-to-hide-existence case here; a `403` always means the grant, never the URL.

The shape of the failure is worth knowing in advance. The GitHub release is created *before* the two
package managers are updated — goreleaser publishes them last precisely because the cask and the
manifest need the release's download URLs — so a token that has gone bad leaves a published release,
two stale taps, and a red workflow run. Nothing rolls back.

The fix is to repair the token and re-run the failed job for the same tag. `release.mode` defaults to
`keep-existing`, so re-running leaves the existing release and its notes alone and re-publishes the
cask and the manifest. No new tag is needed.

The other failure is quieter and is the one the guard in `mise-tasks/release` exists to prevent: the
secret missing entirely. That refuses before anything is built, and names the command to fix it.

## Checking the config without releasing

`goreleaser check` runs on every CI build through `mise run lint:goreleaser`, and fails on a
deprecated property as well as an invalid one — a release config is otherwise exercised once, on the
day a tag is pushed, which is the worst moment to learn that a property was renamed two minor
versions ago.

To exercise the whole build locally, including the generated cask and manifest, without publishing
anything or needing a token:

```sh
mise exec -- goreleaser release --snapshot --clean
```

The cask lands at `dist/homebrew/Casks/harnaas.rb` and the manifest at `dist/scoop/bucket/harnaas.json`.
Both are what a real release would push, with a snapshot version in place of the tag.

content.text:
The release process now works end to end. The credential gap is closed.

## What changed

You enabled the org deploy-key policy; I did the rest.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Credentials** | Two ed25519 deploy keys, `read_only: false`, one per tap — proven by pushing a throwaway branch to each and deleting it, not inferred from the API flag |
| **Secrets** | `HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY`, `SCOOP_BUCKET_DEPLOY_KEY` on `harnaas/harnaas`, piped from file so neither key entered this transcript |
| **Config** | `.goreleaser.yaml` pushes over SSH per tap; `release.yml` passes both secrets; `mise-tasks/release` guard names whichever is missing |
| **Local key copies** | Destroyed — the secrets are the only copies |

Each key authenticates as exactly its own repo (`Hi harnaas/homebrew-tap!` / `Hi harnaas/scoop-bucket!`), so the cask credential cannot write the bucket. And unlike a token, neither expires — which removes the silent failure I flagged earlier, where `brew upgrade` just keeps reporting the old version.

## A regression I introduced and fixed

Swapping the token for `private_key` broke credential-free snapshots. A token resolves when the tap is *pushed*, which a snapshot never does; a git `private_key` resolves when the cask is *written*, which a snapshot does every time — so `{{ .Env.… }}` failed with `map has no entry for key`. That would have broken every contributor's `--snapshot` while passing `goreleaser check` and every CI job, surfacing only when someone tried to build locally.

Fixed with `envOrDefault`, verified by running a snapshot with both variables unset, and documented in the config so it doesn't get "simplified" back.

## One operational tripwire

Turning that org policy back off **disables the existing keys**, in every repo, immediately — both taps would stop accepting pushes. It's in `docs/RELEASING.md`, along with the tell: both taps failing together points at the policy, one failing alone points at that repo's key. The doc also keeps the fine-grained-token fallback as a small, specified edit.

## Corrections from earlier

Two of my own errors, both caught and neither acted on: my first watcher reported the policy enabled when it wasn't (`gh api --jq` writes error bodies to stdout, and I treated any output as success), and I'd claimed a bad token yields 404 — it's 401/403, since the taps are public.

## What's left

`gh secret list` shows both credentials, `goreleaser check` passes, shellcheck and mise lint are clean, `dist/` removed, tap repos have only `main`.

Untested is the one thing only a real tag exercises: the actual push during a release. The first tag must clear **`v0.8.42`** — the immutable Go module proxy still resolves `@latest` to the seeded entire.io tag.

Modified: `.goreleaser.yaml`, `.github/workflows/release.yml`, `mise-tasks/release`, plus new `docs/RELEASING.md` and a link from README. Your `feat/install-and-lint` WIP is untouched. Nothing is committed — say the word and I'll commit these and cut `v0.9.0`.

content.content:
# A command is delivered as a skill only where the harness can be told not to start it

A command is invoked deliberately by a user and a skill is started by the harness when a description
matches, so harnaas delivers a command through a harness's skill surface *and* writes the frontmatter
setting that stops the harness starting it — the disabling is the whole of that renderer rather than a
detail of it. Devin CLI is the first harness on the roster whose skill format has no such setting in
the vocabulary harnaas writes, and whose invocation modes are both on by default. harnaas therefore
refuses the pairing: a command reaches a harness through its skill surface only where harnaas can also
silence it there, and where it cannot, the pairing is reported unsupported and nothing is written.

## Considered Options

**Emulate anyway and state the caveat in the install report.** Rejected because the note is read once
and the file is read forever. The installed skill would be indistinguishable from one the team meant
to be self-starting, and the first anybody learns of it is the harness running a deploy command
because the conversation mentioned deploying — which is the failure the `command` type exists to name
and the emulation exists to prevent. A tool whose purpose is telling a team what is in effect must not
install something whose behaviour contradicts what it reported.

**Write each harness's own suppression key from a renderer per harness.** The right answer eventually,
and rejected here as scope rather than as direction. It needs a second renderer, a way for a surface
to declare which one it wants, and an answer to what an emulated command means in the *shared* skills
directory, which several harnesses read and only one of which would understand the key. Stating the
precondition first is what makes deferring that safe: adding such a renderer turns an unsupported
pairing into an emulated one and invalidates nothing decided here.

**Refuse by default and record which harnesses can be silenced.** Rejected because it inverts a table
harnaas already keeps the other way round. The harnesses that do not read the shared skills directory
are recorded as the exceptions they are, and recording suppression as an allowlist would make every
harness added later fail a pairing until somebody remembered to enable it — a silence that reads as a
missing surface rather than as a missing entry.

## Consequences

The default is that a harness honours the setting unless it is recorded as not honouring it, which is
the same shape as the shared-skills table beside it and carries the same cost: a harness added without
that check gets a command emulated with a key it may ignore. The cost is accepted because the entry is
one line in one file, and because the alternative fails the harnesses that would have worked.

A team declaring commands and adding a harness that cannot be silenced gets one unsupported pairing
per command, reported with its reason while every other target of the same asset installs. No manifest
edit fixes it, which is deliberate — the remedy is a change to harnaas rather than a change the reader
is told to make to a file that is already correct.

The refusal for a harness with no skill surface at all is kept separate, because the two say different

feat: add the devin-cli harness, its adapter and the command refusal

devin-cli is the second harness to need per-harness code, and the first where
the roster's answer and the adapter's diverge. The roster records a per-user
location, because a user-scoped skill reaches that harness through
~/.agents/skills/; the adapter offers no per-user root, because the harness
keeps its per-user rules under one home directory and its per-user skills,
personas and memory file under another, spelled differently per platform. So a
user-scoped rule is refused where the directories are known rather than where
the roster is read.

The adapter maps .devin at project scope, a rule at rules/<id>.md and a persona
at agents/<id>.md. Three absences from that table are three different facts. A
skill and an instruction reach the harness through shared locations, so
answering for them would be a second place harnaas decides where a skill lands.
A command is absent because the harness has no command surface at all — what a
user invokes by name there is a skill — and harnaas refuses to deliver one
through that surface rather than emulate it, because there is no key it can
write to stop the harness starting it unprompted. That refusal is ADR 0005.

The persona takes the flat agents/<id>.md spelling rather than the
agents/<id>/AGENT.md directory the harness also reads: where a harness offers
two, harnaas picks the one the report can name usefully.

cd C:/Users/brasp/Documents/GitHub/harnaas && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat: push each tap with its own deploy key rather than a shared token

The Homebrew cask and the Scoop manifest land in two repositories the
workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN cannot reach, so the release needs a credential of
its own. It now carries two, one per tap, pushed over SSH.

That is two properties rather than one. A deploy key reaches exactly one
repository, so the credential that writes the cask cannot write the bucket and
neither grants anything else in the organization — a token granting Contents:
write on both would have no such seam. And a deploy key does not expire, where
a token does: the release that first met an expired one would be the release
that published the archives and silently left both package managers on the
previous version, which is the failure hardest to notice, because brew upgrade
simply keeps reporting the old version.

The guard in mise-tasks/release now names whichever key is missing, and reports
both in one run rather than stopping at the first, for the reason harnaas
accumulates validation violations: two missing secrets are one trip to the
settings page, not two.

envOrDefault rather than a bare .Env lookup is load-bearing and is the one way
this differs from the token it replaced. A token was resolved when the tap was
pushed, which a snapshot never does; a git private_key is resolved when the
cask is written, which a snapshot does every time. So .Env fails a
credential-free `goreleaser release --snapshot` with "map has no entry for
key", and defaulting to empty is what keeps a contributor's local build
working. Nothing reaches a publish holding an empty key, because the guard
refuses before goreleaser is started at all.

docs/RELEASING.md records the setup, the organization policy the keys depend
on, how to rotate one, and the token form to fall back to.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
